desc:
A grid holds 0 for an open cell and 1 for a wall. You start at the top-left cell and want to reach the bottom-right cell, moving one step at a time up, down, left or right. You are allowed to walk through walls, but you may enter at most k wall cells in total over the whole trip (each time you step onto a wall cell counts as one, even if you have stepped onto that same cell before).

Return the minimum number of steps from the start to the goal, or -1 if it cannot be done. When the grid is a single cell the answer is 0.

grid = [[0,1,1],
        [1,1,1],
        [1,1,0]]

k = 3  ->  4      (right, right, down, down crosses 3 walls)
k = 2  -> -1
hints: Plain BFS on cells is not enough: reaching the same cell with different numbers of walls left leads to different futures.
Make the state (row, col, walls already used) and run BFS on those states. The step count is the BFS layer.

If k is at least rows + cols - 3, a monotone path (only right and down) never needs more than that many wall cells, so the answer is simply rows + cols - 2. For smaller k, remember for each cell the largest number of breaks still available when you got there, and only continue if a newcomer has strictly more.
editorial: Add a third coordinate to the node: the number of walls broken so far. Moving to an open cell keeps it, moving onto a wall cell raises it by one, and states with more than k are illegal. All moves cost one step, so BFS over these states returns the minimum.

The state space is rows × cols × (k + 1), which can be large if k is big, so use two simplifications. First, the shortest conceivable path is the Manhattan route of length rows + cols - 2, and it passes at most rows + cols - 3 wall cells (start and end are open); if k reaches that number the answer is exactly that distance. Second, keep for each cell the best (largest) number of breaks remaining ever seen and only push a new arrival when it improves this value; an earlier arrival with at least as many breaks left dominates a later one.
With k capped at rows + cols - 3 the work is O((rows × cols) · (rows + cols)), which is fast enough for a 40 × 40 grid.
